summary:
Belgium is among the more protective jurisdictions in Europe for transgender visitors. Discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are prohibited; same-sex marriage and adoption are legal; and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination.

Since 1 January 2018, under the Law of 25 June 2017, transgender people have been able to change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, without medical conditions. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the current procedure.

Hate crime and hate speech on grounds of gender identity are criminal offences, and transphobia is recorded as a hate-crime motive. One qualification matters for expectations of the justice system: the OSCE/ODIHR national framework page states that hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and that no code exists to record them as such, so breaches of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions.

Belgium passed Europe's first femicide law in 2023, covering all gender-based homicide and including protections for gender minorities, and a 2023 law banning conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

The principal visitor-facing risk is violence rather than law. The equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men reported in May 2025 that violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people are rising, with gay men and transgender people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. An RTBF investigation documented a recurring pattern in which perpetrators use fake dating-app profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations to rob, humiliate or assault them; police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported through fear or shame. A case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to the Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

The formal-law position is confirmed by the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page, which scores Belgium across legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality and non-discrimination, family law, civil society, asylum and intersex protection.
tangentialFactors:
The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement underway, a contrast with several neighbouring jurisdictions where facilities rules, repeal attempts or repeal reviews are live questions.

Visitor-facing commentary consistently rates Belgium as one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers, and notes a visible queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège. That reputation sits alongside the documented rise in dating-app-linked assaults reported by Unia and RTBF, so a favourable general image should not be read as an absence of targeted violence.

The 2023 conversion-practices ban and the femicide law extend protection beyond the criminal-law core, while the intersex position remains the weakest element of the framework: non-consensual surgery on intersex infants is still lawful despite the Brussels court judgment against a hospital.
localsOnly:
Changing gender registration on an identity card in the Brussels-Capital Region is handled free of charge, with 3-6 weeks processing, requires a valid identity document and an application in person at the commune (a digital mode is available), and according to that regional page requires a medical certificate attesting to sex change and possibly a judicial or administrative decision.

The 2017 law was framed by Justice Minister Koen Geens as placing self-determination at the centre: gender change through a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions, including sterilisation and surgery, scrapped, alongside a reflection period and public-order safeguards. Requests to change name rose from 85 in 2012 to 187 in 2016.

The Institute for the Equality of Women and Men published 'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later' (Motmans, Wyverkens, Defreyne et al., 2017), a large survey of trans people covering coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, official registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Reporting channels for homophobia and transphobia are documented in national guides, and the equality body Unia handles discrimination complaints, including the sexual-orientation caseload cited above.
